title: RNA-Lexis: a probabilistic algorithm using a non-parametric segmentation logic to detect meaningful sequences in RNA.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Downloaded and unzipped the Zenodo code archive (2.97 MB, RNA_lexis v0.2.4, MIT licence): 40 files, of which the only data are two FASTA sequence files (NORAD human 5,401 nucleotides, NORAD mouse 4,945 nucleotides, 1 sequence each). Listed all 9 files in PRIDE PXD076018 via the EBI (European Bioinformatics Institute) API: six Thermo .raw instrument files of 651-772 MB each, one 3,948 MB zip, and two small design files. Read the sample design table (sdrf.tsv): exactly 6 runs = 3 SNHG14 RNA pulldowns vs 3 random-shuffled-RNA controls, all in one cell line (LN-229 glioblastoma). Unzipped the Europe PMC supplement (13.9 MB): a single 24-page PDF of figures, no machine-readable tables.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: The synthetic benchmark (800 transcripts with planted cores plus 200 random controls; 500 sequences of 500 nucleotides with a planted 12-nucleotide motif) is described in the methods but I found no deposited file or generator script for it in the code archive. The four analysed transcripts (XIST, NORAD, SNHG14, LINC01001) are named as Ensembl links; I did not re-fetch them, but they are single sequences. GRID-seq chromatin-contact comparisons and the histone-binding result are reported in the text only; no processed protein table under the 50 MB cap exists in PRIDE.

a1_downloadable.note: Code downloads freely from Zenodo (MIT licence) and PyPI; four transcript sequences are public in Ensembl. But the only deposited measurements, the pulldown mass spectrometry, are raw instrument files (6 x ~700 MB) plus a 3.9 GB zip, all over the 50 MB cap and excluded by the no-raw-mass-spec rule; no processed protein table is provided.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: FAIL and the reason evaluation stopped. Nothing in this paper's deposited files contains a prediction target: the Zenodo archive is source code plus two FASTA sequences, the supplement is a figure PDF, and PRIDE holds unprocessed spectra. Any label (motif functionality, protein binding, localisation) would have to be built from scratch out of other databases.

a3_inputs_present.note: Sequences themselves are present rather than referenced for NORAD (two FASTA files I opened); the other three transcripts are one Ensembl REST call each. Inputs are the only part of a feature/label table that exists.

a4_units_stated.note: Not applicable in the usual sense: there is no measurement table and therefore no units column. The mass spectrometry would need MaxQuant label-free quantification intensities, which are not deposited in processed form.

a5_enough_rows.note: FAIL, verified. Four real human transcripts analysed; two of them shipped as FASTA. The experimental arm is 6 mass spectrometry runs (3 pulldown, 3 control) in a single cell line. Far below the ~1,500-row or ~400-row-classification bar.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: ~3 MB of code plus ~10 kB of sequence; the PRIDE raw data is ~8 GB and would not fit the policy, but is not needed.
a6_fits_laptop.note: The tool itself runs on a laptop CPU in seconds to minutes on single transcripts; size is not the problem here.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: What is deposited matches the paper: NORAD FASTA length 5,401 nucleotides matches Ensembl ENST00000565493, and the 6 PRIDE runs match the described 3-versus-3 pulldown design. The 800+200 synthetic benchmark is simply absent rather than contradictory.

a8_label_provenance.note: The only available 'labels' are defined by the method itself. xmotifs and cores are outputs of RNA-Lexis computed from the input sequence, so training on them means distilling the algorithm, not learning biology; the synthetic benchmark's labels are planted by construction. This is textbook leakage-by-construction.

existing_models.name: RNA-Lexis (this paper's own algorithm, a rule-based segmenter that extends recurring sequence seeds)
existing_models.score_and_split: On its own synthetic benchmark (800 planted-core transcripts, 200 random controls) the authors tuned minimum core length 3-14 nucleotides and report recall, precision, specificity and F1, picking the default by best F1; on real data it is evaluated only anecdotally on 4 transcripts.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: The abstract states plainly that the method nominates candidates and that 'biological function remains dependent on orthogonal experimental validation' - i.e. linking a discovered motif to a function is the unsolved part.

existing_models.name: MEME and STREME (MEME Suite motif discovery, probabilistic and discrete models)
existing_models.score_and_split: STREME (Bioinformatics 2021) is the standard comparator and was used as the comparison in this paper's own simulation on a 60-sequence corpus; MEME Suite handles hundreds of thousands of sequences and motif widths 3-30.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Variable-length and long motifs, and motifs in single sequences rather than corpora, remain hard for position-weight-matrix methods.

existing_models.name: RNALoc-LM (RNA subcellular localisation predictor built on RNA-FM, an RNA language model)
existing_models.score_and_split: Reported in Bioinformatics 2025 to outperform earlier methods on a benchmark of 1,003 long non-coding RNAs, 1,124 microRNAs and 27,682 circular RNAs from RNALocate; split details not read beyond the abstract.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Interpretability - which sequence motifs drive the prediction - is presented as the open question they partly address via attention.

existing_models.name: LncLocFormer (transformer for multi-label long non-coding RNA localisation) and RiNALMo (650-million-parameter RNA language model pretrained on 36 million non-coding RNA sequences)
existing_models.score_and_split: LncLocFormer (Bioinformatics 2023) reports state-of-the-art multi-label localisation accuracy; RiNALMo (Nature Communications 2025) reports state-of-the-art structure prediction generalising to unseen RNA families. Splits not verified beyond abstracts.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Both name generalisation to unseen families and to function (as opposed to structure) as open.

backbone.name: RNA-FM or RiNALMo (RNA language models with open weights) would be the natural backbone for any lncRNA sequence task
backbone.hardware: Frozen embeddings of a few thousand lncRNAs are feasible on a laptop CPU, though long transcripts (>4,000 nucleotides) need chunking.
backbone.licence: RNA-Lexis code is MIT; RNA-FM weights are open. Licence is not the obstacle here.

integration.partner_dataset: RNALocate v2 / NPInter / POSTAR (RNA-protein binding) joinable on Ensembl transcript identifier, which this paper does use.
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Do the variable-length recurrent elements RNA-Lexis finds predict where proteins actually bind a long non-coding RNA, measured independently by crosslinking experiments? - a real question, but it would be answered using those other databases, with this paper contributing only a feature extractor and 4 example transcripts.

controls.positive_control: NORAD's roughly a dozen Pumilio Response Elements (consensus UGUANAUA) are a genuine built-in positive control, and the bundled FASTA exists precisely as a smoke test - but it is one sequence, not a dataset.
controls.negative_control: The paper's own 200 random-control transcripts and the 3 random-shuffled-RNA pulldown controls; neither is deposited as a usable table.
controls.external_validation: None available from this paper; would have to come entirely from RNALocate, POSTAR or similar.

honest_claim_h3: Nothing can honestly be claimed from a model trained on this paper's data, because the paper deposits an algorithm plus four example sequences and six unprocessed mass spectrometry runs, not a set of labelled examples.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use the recurrent variable-length sequence blocks a new algorithm finds in long RNAs to predict where proteins bind them.
plain_idea.train_on: The project I considered would feed each long non-coding RNA's sequence, summarised as the algorithm's discovered motif blocks, to a classifier. This paper supplies exactly 4 such RNAs (2 as FASTA files I opened), so the examples would all have to come from elsewhere.
plain_idea.predict: Which regions of a long non-coding RNA bind protein. The true answer would come from crosslinking-immunoprecipitation experiments in public databases, not from this paper, whose only measurement is one pulldown experiment (3 vs 3 runs) in one glioblastoma cell line.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Labs studying long non-coding RNAs currently guess which fragment to delete or pull down; a reliable motif-to-binding map would pick the fragment for them. But this paper's files cannot test that - it is a tool paper, so the answer would be a verdict on the tool, not on the biology.

more_or_better_data.why: This paper deposits 4 transcript sequences and 6 raw mass spectrometry runs. MEME/STREME run on hundreds of thousands of sequences, and RNALoc-LM's benchmark alone has 1,003 long non-coding RNAs plus 27,682 circular RNAs. We would have strictly less data, not more.

confidence_score.why: There are only 3 biological replicates on one RNA in one cell line, which cannot support per-prediction calibrated uncertainty, and the measurements are not even deposited in processed form.

models_beatable.why: RNA-Lexis itself is a 2026 rule-based segmenter tuned on its own synthetic benchmark and evaluated anecdotally on 4 real transcripts, so a learned model would likely beat it - but a win against a tool on a benchmark the tool's authors invented is not a result anyone needs.

guaranteed_improvement.why: Fails the first condition: there is no shared labelled evaluation set to run the existing model on, because this paper provides no labels at all. Any comparison would be on a dataset we assembled ourselves, on which no published number exists.

ml_idea: Considered and rejected: use RNA-Lexis xmotifs/cores as interpretable features to predict protein binding or subcellular localisation of long non-coding RNAs, benchmarked against k-mer features and a frozen RNA language model (RNA-FM). The idea is reasonable but it needs RNALocate/POSTAR for labels and GENCODE for sequences; this paper would contribute only a pip-installable feature extractor and 4 case-study transcripts, so it is not a candidate dataset.

effort.compute_note: Estimated, not timed: the only deposited data is ~3 MB of code and ~10 kB of sequence, so compute is trivial; the 8 GB of raw mass spectrometry in PRIDE is both over the size cap and excluded by the no-raw-mass-spec rule. No feature table can be built, so embedding and cross-validation times are undefined.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Count the labelled rows the paper deposits. Answer: 4 transcript sequences and 6 mass spectrometry runs, with zero outcome columns. That check took one download and killed it.

verdict_reason: A methods/tool paper, not a dataset. Verified in the files: the Zenodo archive is MIT-licensed source code whose only data are two single-sequence FASTA files (NORAD human and mouse), the 13.9 MB supplement is a 24-page figure PDF with no machine-readable tables, and PRIDE PXD076018 contains only raw Thermo spectra (6 files, 651-772 MB each, plus a 3.9 GB zip) from a 3-versus-3 pulldown in one cell line. Fails A2 (no prediction target is a column anywhere), A5 (4 real transcripts analysed) and A8 (the only candidate labels, xmotifs and cores, are computed from the input sequence by the method itself, so a model would distil the algorithm rather than learn biology). The underlying idea - do recurrent variable-length RNA elements predict protein binding - is a fair question, but answering it would use RNALocate/POSTAR/GENCODE, with this paper supplying only a pip-installable feature extractor.
